title: Making a Living
objectives: I can explain how people earn, spend, and invest money using ten economics words.
I can describe forces such as scarcity, inflation, tariffs, and subsidies that change what things cost.
I can use word families such as consume, consumer, and consumption to understand related words.
I can write a short explanation of an economic choice using precise terms.
rationale: Seventh-grade social studies and current-events reading assume a working vocabulary of economics. This unit sorts the words by role in the economy: people who produce and buy (entrepreneur, consumer, labor, wage), choices about money (commerce, invest), and forces that move prices (scarcity, inflation, tariff, subsidy). Tariff and subsidy are taught as a contrast pair because students often blur a tax on imports with a payment that helps a business. The unit also builds on system and regulate from the systems unit, and on monopoly, so students can describe markets rather than only individual purchases.

words.def: The buying and selling of goods and services, especially over a wide area.
words.ex: River towns grew wealthy through commerce, since boats carried grain and cloth to distant markets.
words.ex2: The local chamber of commerce invited shop owners to talk about bringing more customers downtown.

words.def: A shortage; not having enough of something that people want or need.

words.def: A general rise in prices over time, so that each dollar buys less than before.
words.ex: During a period of high inflation, the same lunch cost more every month.
words.ex2: Because of inflation, a movie ticket costs far more today than it did when your grandparents were young.

passage.title: Behind the Price of a Roll
paras: Teo's aunt Rosa was an entrepreneur. Five years ago she had left her job at a grocery store, borrowed money from a cousin, and opened a bakery on Dalton Street. Teo, who was thirteen, helped on Saturdays, and he was surprised to learn that one small bakery was a piece of something much bigger. Every loaf depended on commerce, the buying and selling that connected farmers, truck drivers, and shoppers.

In March, Rosa called Teo to the counter and spread her supply bills across the glass. "Look at what I pay for flour now," she said. The same twenty-pound sack that had cost fourteen dollars last spring cost nineteen. Prices had been climbing across the region, and the newspaper called it inflation. "My costs keep rising," Rosa explained, "but my customers' paychecks do not rise as fast. If I raise prices too much, I lose them."

A second problem was scarcity. A late frost had damaged part of the wheat harvest, so there was less flour available than bakeries wanted to buy. When a product is scarce, sellers can charge more for it, and Rosa's supplier did. Even her cinnamon rolls were affected. The spice came from overseas, and a new tariff, a tax on imported goods, had raised its price. Teo watched his aunt add a few cents to every roll and wince as she wrote the new sign.

Labor was Rosa's biggest expense, but she refused to cut anyone's pay. Her early-shift baker, Marisol, earned a fair wage, and Rosa said a bakery is only as good as the people who rise at four in the morning. Instead, she decided to invest her savings in a larger oven. It would cost a lot now, but each batch would use less energy and produce more loaves. She had also learned that the state offered a subsidy, a payment to help small food businesses buy energy-saving equipment.

On Saturday afternoon, Teo watched a line of consumers stretch out the door. Each person was making a small choice about where to spend money, and thousands of such choices decided whether a shop like Rosa's would survive. "That is the part the newspaper never explains," Rosa told him, handing a warm loaf across the counter. "Behind every price is a person deciding what to do next."

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "inflation" most nearly means
choices: a sudden sale on flour
a general rise in prices over time
a drop in the number of customers
a tax added to imported goods
qs.why: Rosa says prices have been climbing across the region and that her flour now costs more than last spring.

qs.q: Why does Rosa say she cannot simply raise her prices by a large amount?
choices: She wants to keep the bakery's sign the same.
She thinks customers would stop buying flour altogether.
Her customers' paychecks are not rising as fast, so she could lose them.
The state forbids bakeries from changing prices.
qs.why: She says her costs keep rising but her customers' paychecks do not, and that raising prices too much would lose them.

qs.q: Which detail from paragraph 3 best shows that flour was scarce?
choices: Rosa wrote a new sign for the cinnamon rolls.
A late frost damaged part of the harvest, leaving less flour than bakeries wanted.
The cinnamon came from overseas.
Teo helped on Saturdays.
qs.why: Scarcity means there is less of something than people want, and the frost left less flour than bakeries wanted to buy.

qs.q: When Rosa decides to invest her savings in a larger oven, she is
choices: giving the money away to her workers
spending now in the hope of benefits later
paying a tax on imported equipment
saving the money so that it never has to be spent
qs.why: The oven costs a lot now but will save energy and produce more loaves later.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Bakeries should never hire early-shift workers.
A small business is shaped by larger forces such as prices, supply, taxes, and customer choices.
Entrepreneurs always succeed if they borrow enough money.
Imported spices are better than local ones.
qs.why: The passage connects Rosa's bakery to inflation, scarcity, a tariff, a subsidy, and the choices of consumers.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten economics words in three clusters (people, choices, forces on prices), read a narrative about a small bakery coping with rising costs, use the word families of consume and invest, and write short explanations of economic cause and effect. The unit is designed to be reused in social studies when students read about trade, industry, and government policy.

notes.va.commerce.n: Broader than shopping: it names trade among people and regions. Students may only think of stores; ask about ports, railroads, and online sales. Link to the chamber of commerce, which is a real phrase they will hear.
notes.va.consumer.n: Pair with producer on a two-column chart. Point out that students are consumers every day. The suffix -er means the one who does the consuming; keep the verb consume in the word family.
notes.va.entrepreneur.n: Hard to spell and say; have students rehearse the pronunciation. Emphasize risk: not just owning a business but starting one. A franchise owner may or may not fit; discuss rather than rule.
notes.va.invest.v: Show that investing is not only about money: time and effort count. Contrast with spend. Ask what kind of payoff the investor expects and when.
notes.va.wage.n: Distinguish pay by the hour or day (wage) from yearly salary only if the class is ready; do not overload. Connect to labor history units. The noun has a separate verb use in wage war; leave it for later.
notes.va.labor.n: Multiple meaning: work as an economic resource, versus labor as in hard effort (verb). Students may also know labor from childbirth; acknowledge that and keep the unit sense economic. Pair with wage.
notes.va.scarcity.n: The central idea of economics: wants outrun resources. Students often hear scarce as simply rare; show that scarcity of something people need forces hard choices. Use a rationing role-play with five pencils and eight students.
notes.va.inflation.n: Do not let students conflate inflation with one price rising. Use a basket of five items across two years to show a general rise. Keep the explanation short and avoid claiming causes.
notes.va.tariff.n: Always a tax on imports. Use a simple border diagram. Students sometimes confuse tariff with sales tax or with subsidy; use the misuse sentence to practice sorting.
notes.va.subsidy.n: Contrast with tariff: a subsidy helps and a tariff taxes. Ask who might benefit from a subsidy and who might pay for it. Keep the discussion neutral and invite multiple viewpoints.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The bakery's flour price went up for two reasons. One is inflation, because the newspaper says prices are climbing across the region. The other is scarcity, because the frost left less wheat. Scarcity is about one product; inflation is about prices in general. I need both words to explain what happened.'

Passage is an invented small-business scenario; prices, a late frost, a tariff on spices, and a state subsidy are illustrative, not factual claims about a real place.
